promo-wed-a7.title: Two envelopes, both called A7 #shorts
promo-wed-a7.description:
In America an A7 envelope is five and a quarter by seven and a quarter inches, and it holds a five by seven invitation with a comfortable sixteenth of an inch all round.

Under the international paper standard, A7 is seventy four by one hundred and five millimetres — about two point nine by four point one inches. Smaller than a postcard. Your invitation cannot physically enter it.

Same two characters. Nobody has made a mistake. The word just means two things.

Order the envelope by its MEASUREMENT, never by its name.

promo-wed-measure.title: The envelope has to be bigger than the card #shorts
promo-wed-measure.description:
The sanity check that catches every envelope mistake: the envelope must be bigger than the card in BOTH directions, by about an eighth to a quarter of an inch.

If the envelope number and the card number look the same, stop. If the envelope is smaller than the card, obviously stop.

And when you buy: read the inches, not the letter and number. If a listing does not give a measurement at all, do not buy from that listing.

promo-wed-postage.title: Why square wedding invitations cost more to post #shorts
promo-wed-postage.description:
Square envelopes cannot go through automated sorting machines, so they carry a non-machinable surcharge. So do wax seals, ribbon, bellybands and anything rigid.

I am deliberately not quoting a price, because rates change and the only number that matters is the one at your counter on the day.

So do this instead: make one complete invitation, put everything in it, seal it, and have that one envelope weighed and measured. Then buy stamps. Never the other way round.

promo-wed-date.title: The date on your invitation means two different days #shorts
promo-wed-date.description:
Ten, oh nine, twenty twenty seven. To an American reader that is the ninth of October. To a British reader it is the tenth of September.

On a wedding invitation that is not a typo, it is a guest arriving on the wrong day.

Write the month as a word. It costs you nothing and it removes the ambiguity completely.
